title: Traders brought Central American cacao to Georgia 1,000 years ago
gist: Ancient DNA and chemical residue in 11th-century pottery from the Etowah mound site in Georgia show Mississippian people had trade networks reaching at least 3,000 km to Central American cacao sources, evidence of continent-spanning pre-Columbian trade earlier than previously documented.

insights.claim: University of South Carolina archaeologist Adam King and colleagues found ancient DNA from Theobroma cacao in pottery shards from an 11th-century feast at Etowah, Georgia, implying trade connections reaching at least 3,000 kilometers to Central America, where cacao trees actually grow.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: First direct evidence that the Mississippian culture of the southeastern US had trade links to Central America as early as the construction of Etowah's first platform mound, pushing back the timeline for continent-scale trade networks in North America.

insights.claim: Chemical biomarkers alone (theobromine, theophylline, caffeine, paraxanthine) could not distinguish imported cacao from locally available yaupon holly tea, so researchers had to specifically test for cacao DNA to confirm the trade connection.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Illustrates a methodological lesson relevant to any residue-based archaeological or forensic chemistry: biomarker overlap between local and exotic sources requires DNA-level confirmation to avoid false conclusions.

insights.claim: Chaco Canyon in New Mexico (home to up to 100,000 people at its peak) had well-documented trade connections to Mexico and Central America for goods including cacao and scarlet macaws, unlike Etowah where cacao residue is currently the only such evidence found.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: Raises an open research question about whether Etowah's Central American trade goods flowed directly or passed through the Chaco Canyon/Ancestral Pueblo network, a live area of archaeological inquiry.

insights.claim: The researchers explicitly note that early 20th-century archaeology once attributed Mississippian cultural complexity to Central American influence in a way that denied Indigenous achievement, and that new evidence must now be interpreted without repeating that error.
insights.speaker: Kiona N. Smith
insights.so_what: A historiographic caution about how trade-network evidence gets narratively used — relevant background for how this and future findings will be publicly framed.
insights.quote: This line of explanation was eventually abandoned for lack of supporting evidence and because of the implication that Indigenous people of the Eastern Woodlands were not capable of creating a complex civilization.
